opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the time horizon work is useful precisely because it gives you something you can put on a graph and extrapolate, which most benchmarks don't. A lot of benchmarks saturate: you go from 10% to 90% and then you've learned nothing more. Measuring the length of tasks, in terms of how long they take a skilled human, that a model can complete with some reliability gives you a unit that doesn't obviously top out. And what we found is a fairly consistent exponential trend, with that horizon doubling on the order of every several months over the last several years.

But I'd be careful about how people use it. First, the trend is an empirical regularity, not a law of nature. It could speed up, for example if AI starts meaningfully accelerating AI research itself, or it could slow down if we hit limits in data, compute, or some capability that doesn't scale the same way. So I'd treat extrapolation as a reasonable default with wide error bars, not a prediction you'd bet everything on.

Second, the tasks matter a lot. Our suites are weighted toward software engineering and research-style work that's relatively well-specified and automatically checkable. Real-world work is messier: ambiguous goals, lots of context, coordination with other people, feedback that takes weeks. There's some evidence models do worse on messier tasks, so the headline number may overstate how close we are to automating real jobs. It's also possible the gap closes fast, but we shouldn't assume the number transfers directly.

Third, the reliability threshold is a real choice. The 50% horizon looks much more impressive than the 80% horizon, and for many applications, especially anything you'd hand off autonomously, you need high reliability.

So where I land is: it's one of the better quantitative handles we have, and it should shift people toward taking short timelines seriously. If the trend continues even roughly, you get to systems that can do week- or month-long projects within a few years, and that has big implications for safety and for how prepared we are. The right response is to keep measuring, broaden the task distribution, and build the evaluations and governance we'd want *before* we find out the extrapolation was right.

r001.rationale: The response does not assess AI Futures Project models or say that any are too sensitive to METR’s measurements.

r002.rationale: It says the measured tasks may not represent messier real-world work and cautions that the headline number may not transfer directly.

r003.rationale: It recommends treating extrapolation as a default with wide error bars, but does not advocate using a probability distribution over future capabilities as a basis for planning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is: they should inform forecasts, but with a lot of caveats, and I worry about people over-reading them in both directions.

So just to set up what the measurement is. We take a bunch of tasks, mostly software and research engineering tasks, we measure how long they take skilled humans, and then we look at what length of task a model can complete with, say, 50 percent reliability. When we did that across models going back to GPT-2, we found this fairly clean trend where the 50 percent time horizon has been doubling roughly every seven months. And over the last couple of years it looked like it might be faster than that, more like every four months, though you need a longer run of data before you can say whether that's a real acceleration or noise.

The thing that makes me take the trend seriously as an input to forecasts is just how smooth it has been across very different architectures, training regimes, and labs. That's not what you'd expect if progress were being driven by one-off tricks. It looks more like something steady is going on underneath. So if someone's forecast implies that this trend stops dead next year, I think they owe an explanation of what breaks.

But then the caveats. First, this is a specific task distribution. These are tasks that are well-specified, automatically scorable, and don't involve messy real-world context. We've done some work comparing against real pull requests and more realistic tasks, and models do noticeably worse there. So the headline number is an upper bound on what you'd see in the wild, and the gap between benchmark and reality is itself something we don't understand well. We've also had results like our developer productivity study, where experienced open source developers using AI tools were actually slower, even though they believed they were faster. That tells you the mapping from "can do an N-hour task in a lab setting" to "transforms N hours of real work" is not straightforward.

Second, the 50 percent threshold is a choice. If you look at the 80 percent reliability horizon, it's much shorter, by a factor of five or so. For a lot of economically meaningful work, you care about reliability, not just whether the thing can occasionally succeed. So depending on what question you're asking, you might want to look at the stricter number, and the trend there is similar in shape but the absolute level is very different.

Third, extrapolating a doubling time out five or ten years takes you to horizons of months and years, and at that point I genuinely don't know whether the concept still holds together. Does a "one-month task" even have a well-defined human baseline? Are the bottlenecks still about the model, or about the environment, access to the world, feedback loops? The trend might continue, or the whole frame might stop being the right one. I try to be upfront that the measurement is most trustworthy inside the range we've actually measured, which is up to a few hours.

So how should it inform forecasts? I'd put it like this. If the trend continues at anything like its current rate, then within a few years you have systems that can autonomously do things like the bulk of a week of a software engineer's work. That's a world where AI meaningfully accelerates AI research itself, and that is the thing I most want policymakers and labs to be prepared for, because it's the scenario where a lot of other safety assumptions start to erode quickly. I don't think you should bet everything on that scenario. But I think the data makes it hard to assign it a very low probability, and that should move how much effort we put into evaluations, into oversight, into having the ability to notice when models cross dangerous thresholds before it's obvious.

The other thing I'd say is that the value of this work isn't really the point forecast. It's that we now have a quantitative thing we can track and argue about, where a year ago the debate was mostly vibes. If the trend bends, we'll see it. If it accelerates, we'll see that too. That's a much better position to be in than guessing.

r002.rationale: It says the benchmark uses a specific task distribution, models do worse on more realistic work, and the gap between benchmark results and real-world performance is not well understood.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re a useful input to forecasts, but you have to be quite careful about what you’re extrapolating. We’re measuring the difficulty of tasks an AI can complete, where difficulty is expressed as how long those tasks take a human. That’s different from measuring how long an AI can run autonomously, or how soon it can replace someone’s job.

The interesting thing is that this gives us a way to see progress that’s harder to see on a benchmark where models are approaching perfect scores. You can ask: are they succeeding at tasks that take humans minutes, hours, or days? And then ask what would happen if the trend continued. I think that’s a useful forecasting exercise, provided you make the assumptions explicit.

Reliability is a big part of this. Being able to complete a task half the time is quite different from being able to complete it reliably enough that someone will delegate it without checking. And real work involves ambiguous goals, missing context, interacting with people—all sorts of things that aren’t necessarily captured by a well-specified task.

So I’d use these measurements to inform a range of scenarios, and then look for evidence about whether the trend is continuing and whether it transfers to the work we actually care about. I wouldn’t treat an extrapolated line as a date when everything gets automated. But I also wouldn’t dismiss rapid growth in the length of tasks models can handle just because current systems still make obvious mistakes.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d treat them as one input into a forecast, rather than as a direct clock counting down to some particular level of AI. The idea is to measure the difficulty of tasks in terms of how long they take a human, and then ask how reliably an AI system can complete tasks at that difficulty. That gives us a way of tracking progress beyond benchmarks where the scores are approaching saturation.

But the reliability threshold matters enormously. Being able to do a task half the time is quite different from being able to delegate it and trust that it will get done. And a task that takes a human several hours isn’t necessarily representative of everything humans do over several hours. Real work involves ambiguous objectives, missing context, interactions with other people, and noticing when you’re solving the wrong problem.

So I’d want people to extrapolate with uncertainty, check how sensitive the forecast is to the tasks and assumptions, and distinguish benchmark performance from useful autonomy. The measurements can provide evidence that systems are becoming capable of longer, more consequential work. They don’t, by themselves, tell you exactly when a particular job will be automated or when a particular risk will materialize.
